The story is tightly constructed and deeply unified around the central metaphor of the aging ferry and its motor. The narrative follows a clear, logical progression—the physical crossing of the river—which mirrors the emotional crossing between an aging mother and her visiting son. Every detail serves the overarching themes of aging, loss, and pride: Jonas's wheeled suitcase and his holding onto the railing show how estranged he has become from his childhood home, while Ilse's memories of her late husband Henning highlight her quiet resilience. Most notably, the beginning and the end are bound together in a satisfying circle. The story opens with Jonas's comment that the motor sounds like it is falling apart, and it concludes with Ilse stubbornly offering to take him right back across just to prove that neither the ferry, nor her life on the river, is falling apart.
